meta.title: Who really said "The present is theirs; the future, for which I really worked, is mine"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Nikola Tesla really said it — in a 1927 Politika interview about the radio-patent fight, not in his 1905 wireless-energy article as often claimed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The present is theirs; the future, for which I really worked, is mine'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Tesla — from a 1927 interview on the radio-patent controversy, not the 1905 article it's often pinned to.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Tesla’s own words — spoken in an interview about the bitter fight over who really invented radio, and recorded in Dragislav L. Petković’s “A Visit to Nikola Tesla” (Politika, Belgrade, April 1927). Wikiquote ↗ lists it in its sourced section. The full remark opens “Let the future tell the truth …”; the familiar English wording is a translation from the Serbian.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “A Visit to Nikola Tesla” (interview by Dragislav L. Petković)
From Serbian; English wording popularized via Margaret Cheney’s biographies

source.excerpt: Let the future tell the truth and evaluate each one according to his work and accomplishments. The present is theirs; the future, for which I really worked, is mine.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced section, citing Petković’s “A Visit to Nikola Tesla” (Politika, April 1927) and Margaret Cheney, Tesla: Man Out of Time (2001), p. 230.

The remark is often merged with, or credited to, Tesla’s 1905 article “The Transmission of Electrical Energy Without Wires as a Means for Furthering Peace” — but that article’s verified closing sentence ↗ ends “…only to emerge all the more powerfully, all the more triumphantly from the struggle” and does not contain this line.
Quote sites such as Goodreads ↗ reproduce the line with no source at all, which is how the mis-sourcing spreads.
source.excerptNote: Tesla’s reflection on the patent controversies — above all the fight over priority in radio — that shadowed his later years. The target line is the closing sentence of the remark.
source.rightsHolder: Underlying 1927 interview by Dragislav L. Petković; the familiar English translation appears in Margaret Cheney’s biographies (Touchstone / Simon & Schuster).
source.rightsNote: The words were spoken in 1927 and the original Serbian interview is old enough to be public domain, but the exact English wording that circulates is a modern translation — most familiar from Margaret Cheney’s Tesla: Man Out of Time (1981/2001) and Tesla, Master of Lightning (1999), both in copyright. Treat the English rendering as in-copyright.

author.name: Nikola Tesla
author.heading: About Nikola Tesla
author.bio: Nikola Tesla (1856–1943) was a Serbian-American inventor and electrical engineer whose alternating-current system and pioneering work on wireless transmission helped build the modern electrical age. He spent his later decades insisting that history would vindicate his priority in radio and other inventions over rivals such as Marconi and Mihajlo Pupin — the fight that colours this remark.

misattribution.heading: The words are Tesla’s — but the source usually isn’t
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare feel-good Tesla lines that is actually his. The misattribution here is not the author but the source: the quote is repeatedly pinned to the wrong document.

items.who: Tesla’s 1905 article “The Transmission of Electrical Energy Without Wires as a Means for Furthering Peace”
items.why: Sites including Tesla Universe ↗ attach the “present is theirs” line to this 1905 essay, often bundled with the genuine 1905 sentence about greatness being “ridiculed, condemned, combated, suppressed.” But the article’s verified text ↗ ends at “…triumphantly from the struggle” — the target line is not in it.
Aggregators such as Goodreads ↗ and AZQuotes reproduce the line credited only to “Nikola Tesla” with no citation, which is what lets the 1905 mix-up take hold.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are authentically Tesla’s — but they come from a 1927 Politika interview about the radio-patent fight, as catalogued by Wikiquote ↗, not from any 1905 article.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: By the 1920s Tesla was aging, in financial decline, and publicly overshadowed — Guglielmo Marconi had won a Nobel Prize and commercial fame for radio, while Tesla maintained that his own earlier patents came first. (The U.S. Supreme Court would side largely with Tesla’s priority in 1943, months after his death.)

Speaking to the Belgrade journalist Dragislav Petković in 1927, Tesla framed the whole dispute as a wager on posterity: let history, not the noise of the present, settle who had built the future. The line is less a boast than a bet that vindication would come later.
context.pull: Let history, not the present, settle who built the future.
